title: Incident Reporting & Best Practices
intro:
The entire value of the DevNet programme depends on the quality of the information testers provide. A node crash that is not reported is a missed opportunity. A report that lacks a stack trace or version number cannot be actioned.

This final module covers exactly what to report, how to report it, and what separates a high-value submission from a rejected one.

sections.title: What to Report
sections.content:
REPORTABLE EVENTS BY SEVERITY
Not every node hiccup is worth a report. Here is how to classify what you observe:

Critical (report immediately):
Consensus halt — no new blocks for 10+ minutes across the network
Node producing invalid blocks that are rejected by all peers
Consensus vulnerability — you have found a way to produce a valid-looking fraudulent block
Any event that could allow double-spending or chain reversion

High (report within 2 hours):
Node crash (FATAL/PANIC) with a stack trace
Fork that does not resolve within 5 blocks
Slashing event (SLASHING_DETECTED in logs)
Node stuck on a minority chain (20+ blocks behind)

Medium (report within 24 hours):
Continuous memory or CPU leak (growing over 12+ hours)
Peer connectivity issues affecting multiple testers simultaneously
RPC interface returning incorrect data
Block validation taking significantly longer than expected

Low (report in your next session):
Documentation errors or misleading log messages
Minor UI bugs in the DevNet portal
Suggestions for tooling improvements

WHAT DOES NOT NEED A REPORT
Temporary peer disconnections that self-resolve
Normal WARN log messages
Expected behaviour during announced stress test campaigns
Your personal hardware limitations (slow sync on a low-spec machine)

STRESS TEST CAMPAIGNS
When the DevNet team announces a stress test (e.g., transaction flooding, mempool stress, network partition simulation), you will be given specific instructions. During these campaigns:
Follow instructions exactly — do not deviate
Document your observations throughout, not just at the end
Submit your stress test report via the Issue Council within 48 hours of campaign end
Include exact timestamps, transaction counts, and node behaviour

sections.title: How to Report
sections.content:
THE ISSUE COUNCIL
All reports must go through the Issue Council module in the DevNet portal. Do not:
DM developers directly on Discord or Telegram
Email the team with bug reports
Post issues in public channels

The Issue Council is the only channel that:
Creates a trackable, auditable record
Triggers the reward accounting system
Allows the engineering team to triage and assign
Allows you to track resolution status

ANATOMY OF A HIGH-QUALITY REPORT
Every submission must contain:

Title: Short and specific. Bad: 'Node crashed'. Good: 'pyraxd v0.4.2 PANIC on block import at height 88,421'

Severity: Choose accurately — overclassifying wastes triage time; underclassifying delays critical fixes.

Node Version: Run pyraxd --version and paste the exact output. The team needs this to locate the exact code.

Block Height: What was the chain head when the issue occurred? Check with pyrax attach --exec 'eth.blockNumber'.

Full Log Extract: The 50 lines before and after the error. Not a screenshot — paste the raw text.

Reproduction Steps: Numbered, exact steps to reproduce the issue from a fresh state. If you cannot reproduce it, say so.

Expected vs Actual Behaviour: One sentence each. What should have happened, and what actually happened.

Environment: OS, RAM, disk type (SSD/HDD), CPU cores, internet connection type.

THE REJECTION CRITERIA
Reports are rejected (and earn no PYRX) if they:
Lack a node version
Contain only a screenshot instead of raw log text
Describe known issues already in the tracker
Are submitted for non-reportable events
Contain fabricated or exaggerated data

CONDUCT
The DevNet testing programme is a professional environment. Submissions are reviewed by engineers, not automated systems. Treat every report as a document you would be comfortable with your employer reading.
Do not submit spam reports to farm PYRX — the review team will identify the pattern and it will result in account suspension.

quiz.question: A tester discovers their node is producing blocks that are being rejected by all peers. How should this be classified and when should it be reported?
options: Low severity — report in the next session since the network is self-correcting the issue
Medium severity — report within 24 hours after observing the pattern consistently
Critical severity — report immediately via the Issue Council
High severity — report within 2 hours after gathering a full stack trace
quiz.explanation: A node producing invalid blocks that are universally rejected by peers is a Critical severity event — it indicates a potential consensus vulnerability or a bug that could affect network integrity. This must be reported immediately via the Issue Council, not after gathering more data.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a mandatory element in every incident report?
options: A screenshot of the terminal window showing the error
The tester's IP address and ISP information
The exact node version obtained by running pyraxd --version
A video recording of the issue occurring in real time
quiz.explanation: The exact node version (from pyraxd --version) is mandatory because engineers use it to locate the precise code that produced the error. Screenshots are not acceptable substitutes for raw log text. IP address and videos are not required fields in the standard report template.

quiz.question: Why is it prohibited to report bugs by directly messaging developers on Discord or Telegram?
options: Developers are not permitted to use those platforms for work communication
Direct messages do not create a trackable record, do not trigger reward accounting, and cannot be triaged or assigned by the engineering team
The response time for direct messages is faster, which the team wants to avoid
Discord and Telegram are not encrypted, so bug details would be publicly visible
quiz.explanation: The Issue Council is the only reportin channel because it creates an auditable, trackable record, triggers the PYRX reward accounting system, and allows engineering to triage and assign issues. Direct messages are informal and cannot be tracked, meaning they may be lost and will not generate any rewards.

quiz.question: A report is submitted that says only: 'My node crashed. Please fix.' What is the most likely outcome?
options: It is accepted and the team will ask follow-up questions to gather the missing details
It is rejected because it lacks the node version, log extract, block height, and reproduction steps
It earns a reduced PYRX reward since partial information is still useful
It is escalated to Critical severity because crashes are always high-priority
quiz.explanation: Reports without a node version, log extract, block height, and reproduction steps are rejected and earn no PYRX. The engineering team cannot action a report without these fundamentals. The review team does not follow up to gather missing information — the responsibility is on the tester to submit complete reports.

quiz.question: A tester notices a stress test campaign is in progress. They observe interesting behaviour but decide to wait until the campaign ends to write their report. Is this correct?
options: Yes — final reports are more valuable because they summarise the full picture
No — observations should be documented throughout the campaign, and the report submitted within 48 hours of campaign end, not delayed indefinitely
Yes — submitting during a campaign can interfere with the test conditions
No — reports must be submitted within 1 hour of observing any event during a stress test
quiz.explanation: During stress test campaigns you should document observations throughout — not just at the end. The submission deadline is within 48 hours of campaign end. Waiting indefinitely risks forgetting critical timestamps and transaction counts. Submitting during the campaign does not interfere with test conditions.
